podcast.body: John Denver wrote this song, which became a number one hit for Peter, Paul and Mary in December 1969, their first and only number one hit. He demoed it under the working title "Babe I Hate to Go," and The Mitchell Trio later attempted it before producer Milton Okun gave it to Peter, Paul and Mary. Originally written about a lover's regret, the lyrics gained additional resonance by 1969, becoming a parable for soldiers leaving for the Vietnam War. "He'd even written a song that gave folk trio Peter Paul and Mary a number one hit."

podcast.body: Written by John Denver, this song became a number one hit for the folk group Peter, Paul and Mary in the fall of 1969. It was later the subject of a plagiarism lawsuit against New Order due to similarities with their song "Run." "See, back in the fall of 1969, one of his songs became a number one hit for the folk group Peter Paul and Mary."

podcast.body: Originally a John Denver song, it became a "number one hit for Peter Paul and Mary" in 1969. In 1990, New Order's song "Run" exhibited "Geo-Nee similarities" to this track, leading to a copyright infringement lawsuit from Denver against New Order, which resulted in an out-of-court settlement. "In 1969, one of Denver's songs became a number one hit for Peter Paul and Mary. It was called Leaving on a Jet Plane."
